Market is overreacting to hyperscale credit spreads widening from my perspective. TL;DR Spot pricing for renting GPU compute materially above contracted rates implies hyperscalers are underearning while operating cash flow acceleration is an underestimated source of funds for AI capex.

The fact that spot prices for GPU rentals are at least 2x higher than contracted rates is the missing piece from the discussion about hyperscaler credit, which is the only fundamental factor behind this selloff. Multiple private companies are planning on spending at least 2x more per GPU for compute as contracts roll-off and some have spoken about this publicly.
 
As contracts roll-off, hyperscale growth rates are going to continue to accelerate as their installed bases of compute reprice higher. Hyperscale operating cash flow growth using a mix of estimates and actuals is modeled to accelerate from 31% in the first quarter of 2026 to 50% in the second quarter. This acceleration should continue for the rest of the year and this is not in estimates which incorrectly model a deceleration in the third quarter from my perspective.
 
Some math. Consensus estimates are probably for 25-35 gigawatts added by hyperscale and neoclouds in CY28 (using a range as standing up datacenters is hard and a lot of the neos plus labs are still private).  At 60b per gigawatt, that is 1.5 to 2.2 trillion in capex. Consensus estimates for hyperscale/neo operating cash flow is 1.3 to 1.4 trillion. I think this gets revised up materially as contracts reprice and growth accelerates so the 100b to 700b that would hypothetically need to be plugged by debt goes away. And their credit profiles materially improve. Not to mention the said 100b to 700b would be less than 1 turn of incremental leverage on consensus EBITDA estimates. And obviously the Nvidia and Broadcom “credit wrappers” help improve creditworthiness as well given their FCF profiles.
 
OpenAI, Cursor/Grok and the various Open Source inference clouds have accelerated materially over the last two months per public data and Anthropic continues to grow insanely fast while likely generating FCF. This - along with the fact that spot prices for GPU rentals are so far ahead of contract - are the missing pieces from the BofA chart on hyperscale FCF vs. semiconductor FCF.
 
Hyperscalers are underearning and anyone who signed a contract for GPU compute in 2024 and 2025 is overearning. Operating cash flow will be enough to fund capex but as contracts reprice and cloud growth continues to accelerate then spreads likely come in as well. 
 Would also note that CDS markets are easy to manipulate - was a huge feature of the GFC - short the stock and then buy the CDS. So I would not put attach much signal to CDS.
 Net, net I’m not that concerned about the widening spreads in hyperscale credit. The real risk is that bringing power online and energizing all these GPUs is really hard but we are getting better at this every day.

"One of the things we've learned from crypto over the past decade is that some of the most valuable technology in the world can be completely open source. Think about Bitcoin, Ethereum, Uniswap, Aave, anyone can read the code, fork the code, improve the code. So the code itself is not generally the moat, value accrues to the stuff being built on top, the network, the apps, the liquidity, the distribution, the user network, the community, the brand"

"That's actually very profound, because it's a different model of innovation than what you traditionally see in tech. If you look at what's happening with AI right now, the biggest AI companies in the US are investing enormous amounts in proprietary models, proprietary data sets, chips, infrastructure, and apparently now hardware, which is the subject of this lawsuit"

"So these companies are trying to gain competitiveness from closed source things. That's a really fascinating contrast with crypto, where the competitive advantage often comes from things that everyone can see. It's almost like the total opposite philosophy"

Scientists can now rent access to an automated lab without owning any of the equipment.

Instead of building a facility, a researcher can submit a protocol remotely. Software schedules the equipment and translates the protocol into actions, then returns the results through a structured data pipeline.

For experiments that require millions of dollars in specialized equipment, rented access can be significantly cheaper. Cloud labs have traditionally charged annual subscriptions above $100k. Ginkgo has pushed the model further by quoting individual experiments for as little as $39.

Lower prices open the lab to more researchers but shift more risk onto the operator. The equipment costs the same whether it is being used or sitting idle. Usage-based pricing therefore depends on enough demand to keep the facility busy.

Not all research can be sent to a shared remote lab. Some experiments need highly specialized equipment. Others involve sensitive IP that companies want to keep in house. Providers are responding by focusing on narrower workflows or deploying their automation on site.

Cloud labs could make advanced experimentation available to far more researchers. The real test is whether they can keep expensive equipment in use while supporting the work customers need.

One of the narratives I see people trying to push again on here is memes, and I'm seeing comparisons to 2023. 

I don't see that at all. In 2023 memes were a kind of reaction to the low float high FDV VC scams that had been forced on the market.

They made "sense" as a counter movement to bring order and "fairness" (of course they weren't that fair) back to the market.

It was also the first time the technology got good enough where anyone could create tokens with no real technical expertise and we had a proper scalable L1 in Solana for the first time, so we had a few things combining to create the conditions for an explosion.

Look, I know memes will stick around in one form or another, and are kind of impossible to kill due to the lottery nature and return profile. There will always be a market for lotteries and hope (I'm not bearish Pump at these levels for this reason). 

But, there seems to be nothing new to the approach right now? People are citing that old memes will run again (conditions don't support this), and new ones are reliant on "attention", which is always fleeting. There are no new mechanisms here. We still haven't managed to nail social tokens as a result.

Memes can have a run again in a new bull market if we have excessive liquidity, but this isn't a new narrative to dramatically usher in a new crypto bull run with new entrants. 

You can't continue to play the same game where the end outcome is known by all the existing players, with far fewer players and no new entrants, and expect different results. 

This is the definition of madness.

Way too many people are arguing what the Fed will do by explaining how they USED TO work.

They don’t work that way anymore and now a big “family fight” at the Fed is underway. The repost below is a good read and needs to be understood.

A 35% to 40% probably of a hike is justified. Sure they might raise rates this week, but there is going to be tension and lots of dissents. No hike this week and 50 might be on the table for September.

—-

Years of Trump bashing the Fed has changed them. 

Before everything revolved around the Chair and what they wanted. That is why Wall Street parsed every word and framed every decision around the Chair, their personality and what they believed. The other 11 voters did not matter and were expected to go along with the Chair.

This is not the case anymore.

The Fed is now like the Supreme Court, all independent voters and can out vote the Chair. And there is no more Forward Guidance (signaling what they are going to do.) this is why the probability of a hike tomorrow is 35% to 40%, the Chair could get outvoted and we have no “guidance” either way.
——

All of these changes are positive, and should be applauded. 

The root of many of the Fed’s problems were centered in too much power vested to one person (causing terrible “groupthink”). Additionally, forward guidance that amounted to promises of future moves encouraged too much speculation and leverage among financial institutions as they perceived lower risks creating moral hazards (Fed bailouts for bad decisions.).

These practices had to end.

In the meantime many of the hot takes about the Fed here should be filed under “historical viewpoints” and not “current monetary policy.”

As for monetary policy, it's not just the one rate change that is in question right now, there's multiple:

- FFR changes don't impact things as much when rate expectations are already in line with the move. When it's 99% odds and it goes in that direction, the change is small. However this time, and moving forward, it's 50/50 which means regardless of what happens tomorrow it will be a not fully priced change to the path of rate expectations.

- It's that path of rate expectations that is the crux here not just the one move. Without forward guidance and if they hike tomorrow, there is a good chance that the market will extrapolate that into a series of multiple rate hikes since the market has less to go on. 

- This delta of rate expectations impacts two things: changes in rate expectations do impact the long end of the yield curve. One model for a 10y bond is the present value of 10 years of the fed funds rate. So as that gets repriced, the long end gets repriced. Because hyperscalers have tapped their free cash flow, their main method for funding buildout is in corporate bond issuance. Corporate bond issuance pricing is anchored to the long end bond + a default risk. As yield curve goes up, the cost of issuance will go up making the economics of issuance more tenuous. 

- Increased rate volatility also has an impact on the cost of leverage for things like hedge funds and basis trade. This sits at the foundation of all risk assets since it is the funding leg of margin and leverage into risky assets. Higher variance here = bigger haircuts = smaller position sizes.

Changes in rate EXPECTATIONS, not the realized move, is a major driver or risk assets. I once did an analysis on changes in rate expectations vs quarterly bitcoin returns and the correlation is very high. Attached below. 

In sum it matters because its the whole complex being put into question right now not just a simple 25bps move

Securitize has $4.11B of tokenized assets onchain, and only 0.7% of it gets used.

Maple is a fraction of that size, yet 62% of its assets are actually being lent, borrowed and used in DeFi.

That gap matters because the whole point of putting an asset onchain is for people to lend it, borrow against it and trade it.

RWAs are a $30B market now, and 87% of it is just sitting there doing nothing.

So I stopped caring about who has the longest asset list and started watching utilization, because it tells you way more than market cap.

Here's how the major platforms stack up:

• @Securitize leads institutional issuance at ~$4.11B onchain. Utilization? Only 0.7%.

• @OndoFinance is getting the widest range of assets into 10+ chains , still only ~2.7% in use.

• @maplefinance is smaller, but a much larger 62% of its assets is actually being lent, borrowed and used in DeFi.

Everyone else is basically at zero, so that's not Maple being slightly better, it's Maple running a completely different business.

• @RobinhoodCrypto has a different advantage altogether. It already owns the app, wallet and customer relationship, so it doesn’t need to find users after launching the product.

• Then there’s @HyperliquidX, which isn’t really focused on tokenizing the underlying asset. It’s letting people trade stocks, gold, oil and indices around the clock through perps.

The category split makes the difference even clearer.

Bonds and money-market funds make up ~$16.25B of the market, but only around 5% is active in DeFi.

Private credit is much smaller at ~$3.55B, yet roughly 61% is already being put to work.

So the filter for the whole sector now is who can get RWA assets into wallets, lending markets and trading venues where people actually use them.

And for the tokens, the question is even simpler: when all this activity happens, does any of the money reach holders?

Because an RWA platform can build a very good business without creating a particularly useful token.

$MSFT ’s earnings don’t matter because their battle with the bots is just beginning.

Yes, shares could be up 7% (the implied volatility) but that misses the bigger point:

Microsoft has two major headwinds over the next 5 years, which means it’s likely going to be a value trap.

1) They need to restructure their business model from per-seat to usage-based. Azure will crush it for the next few years, but the core business needs a new pricing model. They hinted at that last quarter and we’ll hear more tomorrow night. New business model = uncertainty = low multiple.

2) The battle of the bots. Even if Microsoft has impressive results the bot boogeyman will not go away. The reason is the utility of software is based on the abstraction layer (the ability of humans to interface with the machine). Agents and bots remove the need for the abstraction layer because they just need bot-talk. I understand how entrenched Microsoft’s products are as evidenced by my daily use of Excel. Unfortunately for Microsoft, “entrenchment” is a relative term when it comes to the power of AI to rebuild business processes from the ground up.

A lesson from the $ 80m+ of liquidations on SKHYNIX perps today: Keep @selenagomez on your mind when you go to trade these RWA Perps.

Perpetual users aren't in the underlying market, betting in the official "casino".

They're the people standing around the blackjack table, betting with each other on what might happen at the table. 

TradeXYZ and other Perp venues go up to them, and offer to referee PvP bets.. for a fee of course.

And as referees they can decide separately from the casino on different rules for the bets, and how to handle all the edge cases. 

If they want people to keep betting with them, these fee charging referees have to try and handle them gracefully otherwise people will find a different place to bet.

So while edge cases get ironed out and Perp specifications of each contract shows itself over time to be Lindy, it is the Wild West and liquidation wicks like today will happen.

As with prediction markets, there can be a difference between being right and getting paid.

"Did Zelensky wear a suit?"

..."Was the SK Hynix pre-open a real price?"

The key part of Perps design is how liquidations are handled. 

Even if Longs are collateralized 1:1, shorts will always have a liquidation point so there is no way to avoid this part of the puzzle.

Over time, refinements happen. Today's SKHYNIX event will make tomorrow's contract better.

Long Term, RWA perps are some of the most exciting instruments in Finance, and as they get refined they will eventually have the robustness needed to drive global price discovery.

Short term...

Whenever you're about to trade a new RWA Perp, remember you aren't Selena Gomez at the blackjack table. You're in the crowd. 

And if the Perp specifications have only been recently implemented, and the underlying is more exotic than a simple MAG7 stock.. well you are actually standing wayyy the hell back in the crowd.

One thing I think people keep missing is that two things can be true at the same time.

1/Compute is absolutely one of the biggest moats in AI. If you don’t have access to enough GPUs, power, networking and datacenter capacity, you’re simply not playing the same game.
2/You can still lose your shirt building that moat.

The internet is a good analogy. Fiber was one of the most important technologies ever built. Without it, there’s no cloud, no YouTube, no Netflix… But a lot of the companies that financed and laid the fiber generated terrible returns. The infrastructure created enormous value, but much of that value was captured by everyone using it, not necessarily by the people who built it.

The interesting thing today is that the hyperscalers are trying to avoid repeating that mistake. They’re increasingly funding their capex with long-term customer commitments before the infrastructure even comes online.

But it’s the AI labs buying that compute that ultimately have to make the economics work. They’re betting their models stay at the frontier long enough to maintain pricing power and high margins. Those margins are what they’ll use to pay for the massive compute commitments they’re signing today.

If frontier models become commoditized, that equation gets much harder. Compute is still a moat, but that doesn’t automatically translate into great returns.

Compute is essential. Great unit economics are not guaranteed. The real question isn’t whether AI needs more compute but It’s who actually captures the value created by all this infrastructure?

This is why retail don't understand crypto, but financial institutions keenly do or any professional that has to deal with risk management on a daily basis.

Many participants, both users and builders, are moving towards Chains that are built on a spectrum of trust minimisation filled with real-world assets. 

Most of these Chains will not be classically cypherpunk, but they will be tremendously better than the status quo of opaque mesh networks reliant on human trust.
